utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning, Professor Bianchini, good morning interpreters. In the technical booth, are you all prepared? So we can continue with the testimony of Professor Bianchini who shall continue to impart to us information about Yugoslavia. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you wish to say anything, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Stefano Bianchini (continued) Examined by MR. NIEMANN:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, just to clear one matter that arose yesterday. I showed you a document marked Exhibit 126 J. Now, that document I think has a document which has been mistakenly attached to it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that the first document, the first page that's the letter from Ambassador Sacirbey, dated the of July, that is the document you had intended to include among the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the document of the 9th of November --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- is not part of what you had intended to include; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document is of some interest, though, I think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it's not directly related whereas it was presented as if it were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think it hurts for the attachment to stay with the document. It may be of some interest, in fact, to Mr. Mikulicic and he may wish it to stay as part of the exhibits themselves, frankly, because it's something that I would imagine the defence would have some use for. So I won't seek to -- I won't seek to have it withdrawn. I'll just leave it with the exhibits, if I may, and Mr. Mikulicic could -- may have some benefit out of it and use it himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now, I think we were approaching the end of the documents that have been tendered, and we got to document 126 S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, perhaps you could put that on the screen for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the last document of the series of documents on international community reactions towards the events that occurred in Bosnia between 1993 and 1994. The document is the number 126 S, and it is a letter, the date is the 3rd of March, 1994. It's a letter signed by both the ambassadors representing Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia to the United Nations, and the document is particularly interesting because it is informing the United Nations that an agreement was joined between the federation and the confederation, the federation in Bosnia between Bosniaks and Croat population and a possible confederation with the Republic of Croatia was joined thanks to the Washington agreement in March 1994. What is interesting again is that the agreement that was imposed by the United States has been signed not only by the representatives -- the two parties in war in Bosnia, that is, in this case, Kresimir Zubak and Mr. Silajdzic as the Prime Minister of the Republic of Bosnia, and Zubak is head of the Bosnian Croat delegation, but also by Mate Granic who was the deputy Prime Minister and the Minister of foreign affairs for the Republic of Croatia, so the document is one confirmation more of the links established between the Croats in Bosnia, Croatia, and the pressure that the international community made on both in order to join an agreement with the Muslims, the Muslim side and the government of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, going to exhibit 126 T, the next exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. This is just -- this is 126 T, it's an article from one of the newspapers. The source is the Times of London, it was published in January of 1994, and informs us that Boban was removed from the talks in -- this was February 1994, so before the agreement, the Washington agreement, was signed. So this is the reason why I wanted to include this document just to inform you that Mr. Boban was not involved because of the pressures of the international community in the negotiation in order to join the Washington agreement. So Boban was removed at the time and then he came to Croatia, and some months later, he was appointed by Tudjman and he received very important role in the petrol company INA in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, would you now look at the document that is being shown to you, and a copy to Mr. Mikulicic, and might it be given the next exhibit number in order? It's just one document. What's the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a decision, an information of the Secretary-General of the United Nations which, on the basis of a series of convention, international conventions, you see from point 1 described here, to point 29, pages 1, 2, and 3, he informed the permanent representative of the Republic of Croatia that the United Nations confirmed to have -- to consider that secessions from the former Yugoslavia take place from October 8, 1991 the date that Croatia assumed responsibility for its international relations, this is written page at 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might just put that on the -- that part, that paragraph, where it is said by the Secretary-General. Could you just display that for a moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you display on the screen --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The part where the Secretary-General makes the comment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He says succession on October 8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, Professor there is attached to it an opinion by Badinter who, as discussed in the course of your evidence, and this is opinion number 11, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Opinion number 11, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take us to paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. This is the paragraph. Even in the case of the Badinter, you have a similar decision, he has written that the same issue is the same as regarding the Republic of Croatia and Slovenia, both of which declared independence on June the 5th, 1991, and suspended the declaration of independence for three months on 7 July, 1991. It is because it was based on the pressures of the so-called troika of the European community, that asked Slovenia and Croatia to suspend for three months, in order to join an agreement. The agreement was not joined. So,<unintelligble> in accordance with the declaration, the suspension ceased to have effect on 8 October, 1991. This is the date on the basis of which the Badinter Commission and the United Nations considered that Croatia took over the responsibility for international relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think it goes on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Only then did these two Republics definitely break all links with the organisations of the federal Republic of Yugoslavia and begin as sovereign states according to international law. 8 October, 1991, is the date of state of succession.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also going back to something you had said yesterday, Professor, in relation to the Vance-Owen Plan, I think that you indicated to their Honours that the Vance-Owen Plan that had been devised in late 1992 and the beginning of '93 more or less triggered events because it coincided with the aspirations of both sides of -- both the Serb and the Croatian side. Just look at these two documents that I show you which I might treat as one exhibit if Your Honours please because they are linked together, but just looking at both, one is an order and one is a decision, Professor, and there are translations attached to both of them. Perhaps they might be the next number in order A and B, if that's convenient to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it will be marked A and B, exhibit 128. The decision will be 128 A and the order 128 B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, dealing firstly with the decision, 128 A, what's this decision? What does it relate to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the decision made by Jadranko Prlic, the president of HVO, the 15th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, Professor, we might be assisted if we have the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, the decision is here. Where on the basis -- on the basis of the partition in ten cantons of Bosnia by the Vance-Owen Plan, as you can see in the point number 1, it is written that all units of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army currently in regions 3, 8, 10, that is the three cantons assigned to the Croats, which were proclaimed Croatian in the Geneva agreements are subordinated to the command of the main headquarters of the HVO armed force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the significance of this? What does this mean, in simple terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This means that the interpretation that was given by the authorities of Herceg-Bosna was that the three cantons considered the cantons with a Croatian majority were Croatian areas. And so in this sense the military, political and military authorities, came from the Croatian structures, Croatian institutions, so Herceg-Bosna and HVO were the right to command and over, for instance, the units of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were considered the units, the army of the Bosnia-Herzegovina state. This means, in fact, they had the idea that a step was made in order to create three states within the Bosnia-Herzegovina state, the Croatian state based on three cantons, a Muslim state, and a Serb state. In this sense, they made a decision and they ordered that all the institutions in a way under the control of other ethnic groups had to be submitted to the commands and the orders and the pre dominance of the Croatian institutions. This is the meaning, in fact,.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to the exclusion of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was treated as one of the three parts, so just as the representative of one ethnic group and not as the government of whole Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next document that's attached to it, 128 B, the order? I think that's linked, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is linked and is the implementation, is linked because, as you can see immediately is written based on the decision of the HVO Croatian Defence council of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is the previous order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the number is the number that you can see on the first page, 01-I-32-93 is the same, so you see this is the decision, the other is the order, coming from the Defence department, and you can see again you have quoted the regions 3, 8, 10.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the three cantons, the three cantons of -- considered as the three cantons of Croatia. You see that in point 3 it is clarified that the HVO main headquarters has authority over region 3, 8, 10 in the municipalities of Croatia and Kiseljak, and the BiH army staff has authority over regions 1, 5, 9, and the city of Sarajevo which were the cantons considered with a majority of Muslim population by the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just on that document that you have been looking at, did that have a triggering effect in relation to the hostilities or the tensions that had been mounting in Bosnia at that particular period in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned yesterday that this had a great impact in worsening the relations between the Croats and the Muslim parties immediately, and the event that created a tragic outlet in this worsening of tensions occurred in Travnik in April, between the 9th and the 7th and the 8th of April, when the flags of Herceg-Bosna were raised on the public buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those flags being raised was really as a consequence of those orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, yes. They wanted to implement this and the reaction of the army was, of course, was negative, and they opposed and they ask -- and they forced to leave out the flags. And around this quarrel -- they are state symbols and you know this is very important particularly in a context of state building process, this has created clashes, armed clashes in Travnik, and the situation immediately was -- influenced all around the area, and a systematic war started instead of remaining just an event -- an event of tensions, as it was the case, for instance, in September, October, November 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're not suggesting, are you, that incidences and military activity on both sides had not occurred prior to April 1993, are you? You're just saying that that was when the main onset of the war --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I wanted just to clarify -- the political scientist's approach as identified, these events related to the Vance-Owen Plan and the beginning of a systematic war between Croats and Muslim units in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But tensions were previously acting. I can just remember the question of the referendum, for the referendum prepared by HDZ in Livno in 1992, in the beginning of 1992, and newspapers reported armed clashes -- conflicts between the army of Bosnia and HVO in the area, particularly in the area of Travnik, Novi Travnik, Travnik, and Vitez, between September and the beginning of November 1992. So there were already -- even reported armed conflict between the two but a systematic war with actions -- with continuous actions had been considered starting from April 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, also in your evidence yesterday you were speaking extensively of the relationship between the HVO and the HV and the linking of the two military institutions. Would you look at the next documents that are shown to you. Again, these are two documents but might be treated as one, if they could? The first is dated the 6th of October and the second one is the 9th of October. I think we've got the wrong documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The documents are marked Prosecution exhibit 129, that is the one of October the 6th, that's 129 A; and the document dated 9th of October, 1992, is 129 B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Professor, do you recognise both these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Firstly looking at the document dated the 6th of October, 1992, what do you say to us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a document -- this is a request for information sent to a series of brigades on the officers -- the Croatian army officers operating in the framework of the HVO. As you see, at the beginning it is written: "Please submit the following information about Croatian army officers in your units," and then the first name, date, personnel numbers, and so on. And then the document says --"inform all the officers that are in the HVO that they can't leave present HVO units without the order issued by the Republic of Croatia Ministry of Defence".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is it signed by? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think this is an interesting sentence that means that the officers operating in the Croatian defence army were -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina had the possibility to leave only -- only -- in the event they received an order issued by the Minister of Defence of the Croatian government, and it says: "If they fail to follow this instructions,<unintelligble, check document> should be forwarded immediately." Furthermore, every Croatian army officer who is assigned to your units must have a written order assigned him to the HVO. You are required to send report and information on every Croatian army officer who arrives in your units." So this means that the flow was controlled -- evidently request of control was made, and then you have copies of the document sent to several brigades or units, military units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think the document 129 B is related?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You have seen the list here of the first document, the document 129 A. You have mentioned, for instance, the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade, Bugjno, and this is the document, following B, is the document received by the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade command, the date is 9 October, this means three days after the first document shown, and this is an order, an order again asking to provide details on members of the Croatian army officers. And as you can see, it's reported more or less the same sentences of the previous document: "Advise all officers they may not leave the present HVO units without an order from the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. They need documents ..." So the second, the third, and the fourth sentences were copied from the previous document. What is also significant is that it is followed by a series of other 14 units. So if you compare the two documents, you have the idea of a kind of network is coming from an order to a certain number of units, from these units to other units. So in this sense, you can have an idea what kind of network was in the system of the HVO army when they received an order about the topic -- and the flows of members of the Croatian army and the acting in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What conclusions are you able to draw as a consequence of looking at these two documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Looking at these two documents, it seems to me that the conclusion that you can have is that every contact between the two army was first under the control of the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian republic, the Minister responsible was Gojko Susak from Herzegovina, so the elements are again confirmed. In a sense you can find also that the relation, the map shown by the OSCE is in a way confirmed, there was a direct connection between the Croatian army and the HVO, and you can see that the participation -- from these documents you can understand that the participation of officers of the Croatian army was widespread indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender those documents, your Honour, Exhibit 129.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, along a similar vein, would you look at the next two documents that I show you, and again two documents but may perhaps be given the one exhibit number A and B. And, Professor, I think very quickly you can dispose of these documents because they are of a similar nature. One, I think, the order of them is the 12th of April, '93, which is an order, and it's signed by Colonel Blaskic, and the second one is also the 12th of April, 1993, signed by Colonel Silajdic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document signed by Colonel Blaskic bears the number 130 A and the subsequent document signed by Colonel Silajdic 130 B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen these documents before, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you in summary form tell us what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very quickly, the two documents are coming -- the first one from Vitez, and this is the document signed by Colonel Blaskic, and the other one is a similar document coming from Tomislavgrad, the date the same, April 12, 1993. So from these two orders you can read -- interesting sentences because they asked for information of the Croatian army officers working in HVO, but they ask included the number, the deadline of the order, and the rank, the number of the soldiers, the first one, while the second one is also asking for -- have a list of Croatian army officers in their headquarters, so it's just -- these are two documents related to what we told before. I can just -- I would like just to turn your attention to the second document because the signature is Zegko Sileg, who signed also Exhibit 129 A we saw previously. This person, Sileg, he was appointed by Bobetko, if you look in the list you can find the name of the persons appointed by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, I tender that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, in the course of your evidence yesterday, you spoke of the situation whereby insignias were either removed in relation to people coming from Croatia and the like. And in connection with that, would you please look at the next two related documents which I now show you. Again, if they could be given A and B references, the first one being an order of the 26th of November, 1992, and the second being an order of the 9th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution exhibit 131 A is the order of the 26th of November, 1992, and the order dated December the 9th, 1992, is number 131 B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise these documents, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you would draw your attention, would you not, to paragraph 3 of document 131 A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is again an order coming from Zenica, dated the 26 of November, and in point 3 is written: Croatian army members present in the region and wearing Croatian army insignia must be warned to take them off as they create trouble for the Croatian Republic, the Republic of Croatia".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any opinion as to what trouble they may create?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that the documents we tendered before about the concerns of international relations can be immediately made in connection with this sentence. So you can see also is -- in point 4 it is added that if they don't have a sufficient quantity of insignia and there is a shortage, the personnel are allowed not to wear any insignia. This is another of the questions that was taken into consideration by the UNPROFOR officers, personnel, when they sent information to the Secretary-General informing him that, if you remember, there were weapons and trucks and soldiers coming back from Bosnia to Croatia with insignia -- or without insignia or with insignia of the HVO which they were supposed to, in fact, be soldiers of the Croatian army coming back to Croatia. This was in 1994, this is interesting because this is the period, November 1992, the following document which is related is of 9 December is coming from another area. This is from Mostar instead of Zenica, it is in the centre of Bosnia. Mostar is near the Neretiva River in Herzegovina so in two parts of Bosnia, and this document, as you can see, is written -- first it's starting again about the insignia and symbols of HVO uniforms worn as opposed to the symbols stipulated by<unintelligble> which as such compromised the reputation of HVO and Croatian army members by implying ideas which the world media may interpret as fascist. This is the order commanders -- commanders of the Croatian communities of the Bosnia<unintelligble> To ensure that the unity members were only having senior and removing all other emblems and then as we can see point 2 wearing HVO insignia is linked to an accusation against the Republic of Croatia and the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna regarding a direct deployment of Croatian army units in the territory of the Croatian community Herceg-Bosna. "Ask Croatian army members with explanation to wear HVO insignia during their deployment in our area". So this is another confirmation that in another part of Bosnia, these orders were distributed and this is in the period November and December '92. In between the clashes -- the incidents, armed incident that occurred between Croats and Muslims in Central Bosnia and the submission of the Vance-Owen Plan and the events that follow. So we are in between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally -- I tender that, your Honour, that exhibit. And finally, would you look at this document that I show you now? This is just one document so ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution exhibit 132.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's the significance of the document so far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The significance is related to the fact that this is a letter certificate on the basis of which Mr. Ivan Antunovic was given, as stated as in paragraph 2 the rank of Colonel and this certificate, this letter, has been issued in order to regulate the transfer from the HVO in Mostar to the Croatian army and may not be used for other purposes. This is a document that shows that it was possible on the basis of this document to make a career in the HVO and then to be -- to transfer into the Croatian army. So this is another document that, from my point of view, shows that HVO and the Croatian army were, in fact, the same army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that exhibit, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, what did the HVO do to the civilian population loyal to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in late 1992 and during the course of 1993 and onwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, generally the -- as we saw in the documents tendered yesterday, the idea was generally to establish a pre dominance -- a predominant control of the Croatian institutions over certain territory, and in this certain territory, all the population and -- the whole population and the institutions had to be submitted to the control of Croatian -- Bosnian Croatian authorities. So in this sense, for instance, they started from the beginning to Croatise the schools or to change topography or to make pressures in order to make clear that the camp -- I would like to use this term "camp," and there's a term in the Serbo Croat or Bosnian languages "Tor", it means closed camps where the peasants put the animals for pasture, and this kind of Tor, closed camp, can give you the idea what was going on in that area. They wanted to create areas where the predominant role of an ethnic group was dominating, so people was compelled to accept these, and they were often forced to accept this situation, sometimes through different actions. Not only through cultural pressures coming from the media, from the role exercised by the parties in this case, the HDZ, or restructuring the system -- the educational system and so on, but even through -- it happened through kidnapping people. Sometimes there were some of these events. And this -- the victims were not any more -- only Serbs. Sometimes they are even Croats too. And this was enough understandable if it means that there were resistance reactions. Even in the Croat population towards attempts at homogenising the group. This is consistent with the logic of the war. I don't know if you ever had the opportunity to see a very interesting movie made by a director -- Macedonian director Mancevski 'Before the Rain' is the title of the movie. This is a movie which explains in a very excellent way how is -- has been prepared before the war the homogenisation in the case of the Albanian and Macedonian groups but the logic is the same, and when homogenisation is joined a certain point in -- enough solid, in this moment you need just an element of -- a political element in order to open the fire and have the war. So in this sense, this was a process that was going on. The pressures against mediations as, for instance, the case of Stjepan Kljujic is significant enough. I can add that during the war, even during the war, it happened this great pressure in order to create conditions of homogenisation and clash of the groups. One of these events occurred in Fojnica. I have documents that show that the command of the HVO in Fojnica, Mr. Stjepan Tuka, didn't want to implement orders from the HVO general head quarter because he had -- he explained these orders will provoke the war in Fojnica between the Croat and the Muslim community. And he was urged to implement the orders, and the battalion, the HVO battalion. The Franciscan Monastery in Fojnica and the Islamic community in Fojnica signed letters and documents together in order to support Mr. Stjepan Tuca and his position. He was compelled to resign, another person came and immediately after this event the war erupted in Fojnica. The OSCE confidential document I spoke about in the last sessions also told the example of Vares where the mayor was Croat and albeit because in Fojnica there were a good majority community of Croats and a great community of Muslims, and they received refugees and displaced people, Croatian refugees and displaced people, from the outside areas in 1993 when the war already was -- erupted in Bosnia, and between the Croats and the Muslims. But the mayor, Croatian mayor, sought to maintain good relations with the Muslim community and he succeed to manage this until HVO armies arrived from the outside, enter in the city, and they compelled the mayor to resign and then the war was provoked. So in this sense you see that two streams even clashed within the Croatian community in Bosnia, and the pressure was made in order to homogenise and create the conditions for a Croatian ethnic areas in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, in the course of your research, did you come across any documentation or illustrations, proposals, to move ethnic populations about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I found -- I found -- this was even -- if I can say proposal coming from a moderate stream of the HDZ. In 1992 -- in 1991, I found a book published in Vitez by Anto Valenta who was the vice -- the Deputy President of the HVO later but not in 1991 when he published the book, and he -- the book was about saving the integrity of Bosnia through moving of population. And he prepared maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might look --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we can tender the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit 124 -- 124 and 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four and five. I don't have the official.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I could mark -- 124 and 5. There's two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is one here. They are related. They were included in this interesting book. As you can see, his proposal was to move a large part of the population you see here, the Croatian from the eastern side of Bosnia moving to the western, and an exact number of Serbs moving from the eastern side to the western side. The same you can see moving population from Muslims and Croats from one side and Serbs and Muslims from the other sides in order to have at least the three parts with a clear majority of one ethnic group, the western side the Croatian group, the centre the Muslim, and the eastern the Serbs as it is even clearer in exhibit 1, 2, 5, when you can see the three colours, blue for the Croats, green for the Muslims, and red for the Serbs, in order to save -- this was his idea, to save the integrity of Bosnia through a moving of population and the creation of three areas with a predominant -- one predominant ethnic group in each of these areas. I wonder that -- the book was published in 1991, as I told you, and later, in 1993, Ante Valenta suggested effectively in really a moving of population in Zenica. The mayor published after the war his memoirs, and through the memoirs it is interesting to know many details in this sense, and he quoted this event when he had this discussion with Ante Valenta who proposed consistently with ideas to move population from Zenica into the cantons or areas other Croatian population -- to move Croatian population into cantons and areas under the control of HVO, and with a Croatian community, in order to avoid any armed conflict in Zenica. The mayor was opposed because he wanted to save at least the inter-ethnic characteristic of the community of Zenica, which is predominantly Muslim, so this was in effect the -- this moving thing was not agreed by the two. But is just to give you also an idea of the elements that were -- and the streams that were acting into the Croatian community and in political circles about the possible evolution of the events of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did the HV/HVO forces during the period of the conflict in 1993 also utilise camps and detention centres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. According to the OSCE document, confidential document, I quoted several times, there were at least 26 detention camps, different levels in -- particularly in -- controlled by HVO. And the most famous were Heliodrom, Dretelj, and Masinski Fakultet in Mostar. These were the most known. So they forced people to stay there in order to punish the representatives of the other ethnic groups and in order to encourage the ethnic cleansing of the areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did the Bosnian Croats in Croatia do with respect to public media facilities, including television, radio, and press?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, before the war erupted in Bosnia, there were particularly a proposal by Velimir Ostojic who was Serb Minister of Information in the coalition government of Bosnia in order to create three ethno national channels of the Sarajevo television and to give one channel to each ethnic group. This proposal was submitted at the end of 1992 -- 1991, sorry, and in January 1992 was supported even by HDZ, but because the three parties could not agree as they are particularly -- was uncertain on this topic. The situation was not completely -- was not solved. And then when the war erupted, war occurred even around the transmitting stations of the media. You know, before the war anyway, the Serbs and the Croatian communities had the opportunity to read amongst the whole Yugoslav newspapers, newspapers and magazine coming from Zagreb and Belgrade. When the war erupted, it was very important for the Serbs particularly, because they started to control the transmitting stations. So they were able to control eight out of eleven of these transmitting stations. Only one was controlled by HDZ, Croatian -- the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, and eight of these nine -- the tenth was destroyed, and the eleventh one remained under the control of the Sarajevo television. This was the situation in the first part of the -- the first phase of the war. Herceg-Bosna later, between December 1992 and August 1993, set up a system of -- an information system, its own information system. August 1993, it's an important date anyway because in August 1993, the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna transformed itself and proclaimed itself a Croatian republic, Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna. So in between this period, between December and April, December '92 and April '93, television was created in Siraj and Briec and according to journalists, in particular to international journalists, the majority of journalists working in ^ were coming from the Croatian television, from Zagreb. Then they created also a weekly and radio in Mostar and, (Croatian name) a press agency, that was the name. In this period they tried to prepare videotape cassette and they sent even this cassette to -- on information what was going on in the Herceg-Bosna to the Zagreb television hoping that they would be broadcast by the Croatian television, particularly in the most popular transmissions as, for instance, Slikom Na Sliku which was very known and followed by population in Croatia. A very well known journalist was Mr. Sagol, he was known particularly because he invented a lot of news according to the journalists, invented the term Sagolica in order to say news and invented news. This is interesting enough because the situation changed after the agreement, Washington agreement, in 1994, and one of the most -- one of the authorities of the Herceg-Bosna, Bozo<last name unintelligble>, accused the journalists not to follow the new stream with the agreement of the Muslim. He changed radically his position and instead of being the partisan of the Croatian Herceg-Bosna, he became immediately the partisan of the agreement with the Muslims. So it's just to give you a short story of what happened in the media. However, you know, the media played a crucial role in order to prepare, to a large extent, sectors of the population to the war before the war erupted and the responsibility, the first responsibility, was in Serbia. Serbia manipulated radically the media in Belgrade in this sense, and then the others followed. And this is, I think, very interesting in order to deepen a specific aspect of the organisation of the consensus before the war erupted. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think that it will be a convenient time for us to take a break now. It is 10.10, so we will take a 20-minute break at this point and then continue. Thank you. --- Recess at 10.10 a.m. --- Resumed at 10.33 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Professor Bianchini, you have now replied to the questions of the Prosecutor, and perhaps now Mr. Mikulicic would like to ask you some questions. Mr. Mikulicic, do you wish to cross-examine the witness? The accused has to be brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by. Good morning, Professor Bianchini. My name is Goran Mikulicic, I am defence counsel in this case, and together with my colleague, Joka, I act on behalf of the accused Mr. Aleksovski. The defence will ask you some questions and ask you to give your comments on some of the documents that you have used in your exposition, and I would ask you to reply to these questions to the best of your ability and conscience. Professor Bianchini, needless to say, it is with great attention that the Defence has heard your testimony as well as -- in the month of February as well as these last few days, and in every respect, it has been a mostly informative and interesting statement. But the Defence has to present, right at the outset, some reservations in respect of some of your conclusions and also its opposition to some of your conclusions, so that the Defence, invoking the documents which you have used in your ex position, will be asking you for some additional questions, clarifications, and comments. But to follow a certain order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bianchini, just briefly, the subject of this case, events which took place in the Lasva River Valley, more specifically in the territory of the Municipality of Busovaca, where was situated the facility of Kaonic in which place Mr. Aleksovski performed his functions. The events which the indictment refers covers the period from the end of the month of February to the end of the month of May in 1993, thus that is the period which is of interest to the defence. Of course, it is not possible to exclude that period without previous knowledge of the previous events as well as of partially knowledge of subsequent events. So having said this, the Defence will kindly ask you to clarify for the benefit of us all and, of course, the Trial Chamber, how come that in the areas of the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we are speaking about a particular locality, how come that in those areas there are persons of Muslim -- of the Muslim faith and what does this represent actually a national entity or a religion, a faith, in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, when you speak about Bosnia and about the role of the Slavs with a Muslim name, surname, and we can say, Muslim religious characteristic which is a little bit disputed in the sense that you can have people claim for themselves to be Muslim but not believing in any god. So this is a very specific situation. Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina are Slavs, generally, they share the same language with the other Slavs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. According to the historians, they were generally persons who shared a different religion, Christian religion in the Middle Ages. They were neither Catholic nor Orthodox, they followed a heretical sect, so-called Bogomil. When the Ottoman Empire arrived, many of them, because they were constantly under pressure both from Catholic side and Orthodox side, they accepted the Islamic religion. And then they evolved, they remained as a population, particularly in the towns and the centres, the cities, instead of the countryside. This was until the 20th century when it started a discussion about the Muslims. Are the Muslims Croats who believe in the Muslim religion? Are the Muslims Serbs who became Muslim because they share more or less the same language? And so you have often publications and books claiming that the Muslims in Bosnia are, in fact, Croat of Muslim religion or Serbs of Muslim religions. And Muslims themselves proclaimed something separate, and they claimed this during the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in the twenties and the thirties and then during the Tito's period. So that they were recognised as a specific community in the context of the resistance movement in Bosnia, the Stavno documents show this very clearly, this was disputed on the Yugoslavia level since they were accepted as a separated community in the '60s. But if your question is who are they originally? This is against one of the questions connected to the idea of nations. Is an ethnic group coming from a conscious decision because they share voluntary certain sects or are they connected through biological origins? You can't find a scientific answer. This is a question of how people understand the question of nations. So if you recognise the right of a group to -- of every group to define themselves as a nation because they share voluntarily a certain set of values, they are a nation, so in this sense, we can consider also the free choice of the person who claims themselves as Muslim. Then, just to make clear, then when the Yugoslav federation collapsed, they made the choice not to be called Muslims but Bosniaks, but that doesn't mean Bosnians, because that means all the citizens living in Bosnia-Herzegovina while in the -- the Bosniaks are those who are not Croats or Serbs or other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Bianchini, observing things through the prism of history, and you mentioned the Second World War, when do we find the first elements of a description of the Muslims as a nation and how was this resolved in the former Yugoslavia through the constitutional arrangements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About the -- I mentioned the document of Stavno, and they included Muslim as a nation in the resistance movement of the Trieste party movement. They are -- you can find also now, you have particularly in Bosnia, a new way of discovering when this nation arose, when the word was used, the existence of the language, of the Bosnian language, as a different language than the Serb and Croat languages, you have publishing of books. As an expert, I don't find this kind of quarrel particularly interesting because I don't think that it's crucial to understanding when a nation starts to exist because I don't share this kind of continuity in the idea of nation. You know, it's true that in the Middle Ages we had a Bulgarian empire, but this Bulgarian empire was not a Bulgarian state in the ethno national sense. The empire was empire, this is crucial. The name was of secondary importance. And so I think this is very important to understand. This is a question of our time, not having, in my opinion, so strong connection with the long-term continuity. It's related to the modern idea of nation and how the modern idea of nation evolved. So in this sense, I think that it -- we can discuss about the Muslims and they are requested to be recognised in -- during the Second World War because we are speaking about the former Yugoslavia, albeit you know that a Muslim organisation, political organisation, existed during the twenties and the thirties in Bosnia and then the Muslim community was not in the beginning recognised as a Muslim ethno nation. In the constitution you can find, particularly in the constitution of 1974, they were recognised after a period of making pressures. So the middle of the '60s was the time when the Yugoslav context recognised the existence of -- recognised the existence of a Muslim community as a nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we could say that, looking at the legal, the legislative, and the constitutional regulations of an ordered society of a state, and here I'm referring to the former Yugoslavia, that the Muslims appearing in Yugoslavia in that particular framework in the 1974 constitution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the constitution? I have the constitution. We can -- if I can -- the constitution of '74, I have. May I just ... I'm just looking at the beginning of the first articles of the constitution, the first part, and it is interesting to see that, for instance, article II speaks about the republics and autonomous regions but is not listing a series of titular nations so you can't have the Muslims, neither the Croats or the Serbs. You have here the republics. I should see if in the articles connected to -- but even in the first principles you have listed the peoples of Yugoslavia and peoples were considered the so-called titular nations but you have no list of these peoples in these basic principles as I'm looking for. You know, it was understandable, the first interest of the socialism was self management, labour, the working class, so you see in the constitution, even in the Bosnian constitution, I have the Bosnian constitution with me, you have first they pointed out the role of the working class and then of the peoples. So in the constitution of Bosnia, you have quoted the three peoples. Here you have not the list, the Yugoslav '74 constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but however, that notwithstanding, we have encountered and you also used in your statement in exhibit 37 -- I should like to ask the usher to give that particular document to the Professor -- so when one looks at this table, which represents the ethnic population in Yugoslavia, one can see that there is a percentage showing the number of Muslims from 1981 till 1990 -- which grew from 1981 to 1991. So we can see that this population features in official statistical data as a population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were as a result of the census, and when the census had to be prepared several times there were discussion whether to introduce the possibility to the term Muslim or not. But in 1991 -- in 1981-1991, there were not discussion about the introduction -- the use of the term "Muslims" in the list so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but is it true that at that time the people, the citizens of the former Yugoslavia, stated their national affiliation in this particular way? And predominantly what areas of the former Yugoslavia did the Muslims live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In, sorry, I understand that your question is, we are speaking about when you use the term Muslimani, you're speaking about the Muslim population, because otherwise --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wanted to make it clear that you were speaking about Bosnia in this sense, or Kiseljak you have some such, but predominantly in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now take a look at another ethnic population group which is involved in the events covered by the indictment. These are the Croats. Looking again at the statistical table, it derives that in these census of the population there were a certain number of the population which declared itself as Croats which was your<?>, but can you tell me in what parts of the former Yugoslavia did the Croats predominately live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They predominantly lived in Croatia. I can be more clear. They were predominantly in Slovenian, in Croatia proper, in Istria in Dalmatia, and in one part of Bosnia-Herzegovina that is in Herzegovina particularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the part that I'm particularly interested in. So you said that at the time of the former Yugoslavia, in a part of the former socialist republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there also lived Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In one part, yes. As I told before, the same was for the Muslims living in, for instance, in Sanjak, so population was distributed in other way, there were also Serbs in Croatia, this was not linked to the territorial -- the administrative territorials. The population lived -- Croatian population lived in one part of Bosnia, yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While it existed, the former Yugoslavia, you partly broached this subject right now, what were the republican borders in the former Yugoslavia, what was the character of those borders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were -- they have -- they have an administrative meaning from the international point of view. They were areas that were a part of the -- of a single state with a unique economic system, with a unique currency, with a unique foreign policy, with a unique defence policy, while -- with characteristic -- different characteristics within. For instance, each of these republics had their own constitutions. The constitution had to be made in accordance with the federal constitution but they had a constitution. They had a different system for education, for instance, or they had their own control on the police through the Minister of the Interior of each of the republics. So they were different -- the borders were administrative borders in a context, in a related context, but each republic had their own peculiarities, their own system, their own legal system and own constitutional system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any administrative barriers in the communication of Croats in Bosnia and Croats living in Croatia and the bordering areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean difficulties in administration plan?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any barriers in the sense of state of -- frontier, border controls, in the system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The free flow of persons was guaranteed as well as all the population in Bosnia went, if you want, to Dalmatia during the holidays, some holidays. Croatian people had the same -- it was for the Serbs or the Bosnians or the Slovenians, people moved freely all around Yugoslavia, for job, for tourism, for different reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have explained, Professor, that due to the collapse of the former Yugoslavia, new states have emerged on these territories on the basis also of the conclusions of the Badinter commission. Now, considering this area where the Croats lived prior to the collapse of the former Yugoslavia of Croatians in Bosnia, what has happened now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is very important question. The answer is what happened? It happened that the recognition was for the republics belonging to Yugoslavia. So republics were recognised on the basis of their administrative borders. This means, if you want, for the Croatian population living in Yugoslavia, that the majority of them were in the Republic of Croatia, the large overwhelming majority. Part of the Croatian population was living in other countries, for instance, Bosnia or Serbia, if you want to take into account, for instance Vienna, and the significant presence of Croats in Srebernica. So this happened to -- for all the ethnic groups of Yugoslavia, the same was for the Serbs. The Serbs became in Croatia part of the population, part of the population of the Croatian state. It was same for the Serbs in Bosnia and you can see the same was for the Albanians and for the Muslims because the Muslims were in the -- in Bosnia but even in Sanjac, that is between Montenegro and Serbia. So this was a common fate of the different ethnic groups in former Yugoslavia when recognition was implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the recognition of the former Yugoslav republics, I'm thinking of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the one hand and Croatia on the other hand, and what were the relations now. So prior there were no administrative barriers and limitations; however, in this new geo-political conditions, what were the relations now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the recognition was implemented by the European union was achieved by the Croatia, it was a situation of war. So it was not a normal civilian context when you establish borders, as it was the case, for instance -- in this case, a little bit different was the case when Slovenia establish its own borders on the Slovene Croat borders because the war erupted two days later. But they were already prepared to establish their control on the Croat-Slovene borders, and it was a shock for the Croatian population living there because particularly in Istria they were used to move from one side to another, for job. Suddenly, from one day to another, they became foreigners of this country. And, of course, from the legal point of view, it was the same for the population in Bosnia and the population in Croatia. However, you can't forget that Croatia was involved in the war. One part of the huge territory was under the control of the Serbs irregular units, I mean Krajina, and part of Slovenia, and communication was radically difficult, and Bosnia in that time, I mean between the beginning of the war in 1991 and the recognition of Bosnia, April 1992, lived in a context which was in between the -- to become sovereign state and to be part of the still existing socialist Yugoslav federation because the socialist Yugoslav federation disappeared. In fact, when -- from the political point of view, Ante Markovic gave his resignation in 1991. From the legal point of view, I think it was when Serbia and Montenegro declared on April 27, 1992, their federation. So this was the end of this process of dismemberment of whole Yugoslavia, so in this sense I think that the situation of the population had to be considered in the framework of this difficult and specific situation and not peaceful situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this light, would it be possible to conclude that in the course of 1992 and 1993, the process of adjustment and the creation was still in course, that not all of those structures have been set up which exist in a stable state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you speak about -- about a real context, a real situation, of course it was the situation. It was a war, and you had -- and you had people going -- coming from one party to another because there were claims for change in territories, of former Yugoslavia. But from the international point of view, the recognition was very clear and was related to the administrative borders of the republics of Yugoslavia which were considered international borders, and in this sense, in this sense, international community all the times interpreted the recognition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Understandably so. But with the international act of recognition, that day itself, it was the 6th of April in 1993, Bosnia-Herzegovina is a sovereign state, did it have the possibility to control all its borders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that generally speaking, in a context where the sovereignty of Bosnia was not threatened by Serb side, Bosnia had the possibility to control in a few days its borders. The problem was that it was made difficult this because of the -- because of the claims coming from -- immediately coming from the Serb side. We have to take into account that in this sense, Bosnia could rely on the help of the international community taking into account that the recognition happened after the deployment of UN armies in Krajina, the peacekeepers, so in this sense even the borders between Krajina and Bosnia was, in a sense, under the control and the protection of the UN peacekeepers who arrived at the beginning of April, just in the moment when the recognition was made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, considering this problem, throughout history we were faced with similar situations. I am referring to a situation where due to certain administrative solutions, as a consequence of bilateral accords or as a consequence of certain world or international conferences, the Versailles conference, for example, when you have a new state and territorial division, it is usual that for a population which remains "enslaved" in some other country, that the mother country maintains relations with that population remaining outside its borders? You mentioned Istria, in Istria an important Italian minority lives. We know about the annexation of Istria, the First World War and so on and so forth. I won't go into that. It is true that the republic of Italy today maintains the contacts with this Italian minority living in the Istrian region, both of Slovenia and Croatia? Is it also true that in Trieste, an Italian city, there is an important Slovene minority with its cultural organisation which has close contact, has close links with the mother country, Slovenia. Would you comment that in connection with Herzegovina, the recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Croatia, and the national entities living on these territories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a very interesting question. And it's a good comparison, in a sense. In a sense that you see we have to take into consideration what is the role of minorities in this context. It is true that Italy takes care of its own<?> but this happened today in this context through bilateral agreements. Italy and Croatia, Italy and Slovenia, have a certain kind of agreement in order to protect each other their minorities, and when one minority is not being protected is a matter of negotiations. When this didn't happen -- it was the case, for instance, Istria -- Italy not Istria -- we can add Dalmatia, Italy, for instance, as I said in February, Dalmatia was used, manipulated, by Italian policymakers in order to dismember Yugoslavia or to take one part of the territory which was <indescernable> at the time as today an overwhelming majority of Slavic population. So this is the question. It depends on the nature of the attitude of each state when considering the role of the minorities. In principle, each state has a right of helping, giving protection, sending economic support for certain activities, but this is only a matter of negotiation, bilateral agreement, in order to guarantee the other state that this is not against him, is just for protecting a minority in a sense to helping a minority to maintain contact with the so-called mother nation, if you want. So it depends how you use the question of the minorities. You know that this was also for Istria a subject of many tensions between Italy and Yugoslavia even after the Second World War. At least until 1954 when the so-called territory, free territory of Trieste was divided, definitely in a zone A and zone B; zone A assigned to Italy and zone B assigned to Yugoslavia. And it started again a difficult process of re-establishing confidence measures and negotiation in order to -- so this is a matter under these conditions that can be considered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do understand. By interpreting this answer of yours, we may conclude, and if I err, please correct me. We are speaking here of a long-term process, and when speaking of history in other cases, when we have a peaceful context, here, on the other hand, in connection with this indictment, we have a short period of time and a period of war. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends if -- these matters can be even to a certain extent very rapidly be negotiated. The problem is, if the state has or not -- and the policymakers have or not a peculiar attraction toward nationalism, if they have a peculiar attraction toward nationalism, this process will take a long time. If they don't have, it should be immediately created a fundamental prerequisite for a rapid solution of the question. So it depends. We have to consider the different period. Italy had a very strong nationalist approach, but take into consideration the -- even difficult -- recently, difficult relation for a certain period with Slovenia because of the question of Bosnia Slovenia. One government of Italy was nationalisticly oriented and this created a lot of problems with Slovenia. When this government was removed and another one took over the power, the negotiations and the solution was found in a few months. So this is the reaction that you can have if the ideology of reference, if I can say, of the policymakers of a state is related or not with the idea of nationalism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So linking this question, let us now focus on the question of political organisations of the population in both of the two countries. I am thinking of the predominant party in Croatia and in that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I am speaking of HDZ. May I ask you: Do you know, Sir, that the party links in some cases exceed the state borders and parties establish common links on a different level of the same identical programs, political -- identical political ideas, political procedures. Tell me, do you know of such a case in contemporary Europe and history of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you want to take into consideration, for instance, the social democrat relations of the parties or the Christian democracy parties, they had their own different parties coming from different countries with meetings, international meetings, different -- sometime different, sometime close programs, but in a multi-international environment. There were not two -- there were 10, 15, 20 organisations that they found. Sometimes there was one party trying to establish his own control over the others. This was the case, for instance, of the Communist International. But this is a specific case. Specific case because Communism, as it was the Soviet Union, let's say Stalin, was to create the conditions for a revolution in the world. They wanted Lenin, Trotsky, in 1917-1918 -- when communism was created, they wanted to provoke the war, and they hoped to have the revolution, the world revolution, in the sense in Germany, in Great Britain, in France, and they interpreted the Soviet revolution in Hungary, the so-called<Italian term used> in Italy, the Red Vienna, the Sparticista<?> Revolution in Berlin as the signs of this, and this is one thing. Then arrived Stalin. Stalin interpreted a different sense this. He had the idea that Soviet Union was besieged, that the Soviet Union had to be protected by the other communists, and he manipulated the Comintern in order to transform it as a tool for dominating the other parties. What was the outcome of this attempt? That step by step all these parties clashed with Soviet Union and Comintern<?> was closed, dismembered, in 1943, the attempts to create a new organisation failed in a few months because the clash between Tito and Stalin showed that this was impossible. So in this case, you don't have this. It's very peculiar. You have -- these organisation -- this is also interesting -- are a political organisation of political parties sharing similar -- similar -- political ideas. They are not related to each other for ethno-national reasons, and-- these are very important questions. Then they failed, they were unable to find a strong organisation. This is other matter. This is related to the relations between -- amongst these parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Professor Bianchini, I would kindly ask you to go through the exhibit and every time that I quote one of the exhibits, I will ask the usher to present that to you so that you can show it to -- on the ELMO. Exhibit 38, please. You can see again a statistical table which compares the ethnic population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so the Muslim population is the predominant population in that territory. The Serb population is represented with -- the Croat population is represented with some 18 percent, approximately. That is twice less than Muslim population. Would it be therefore correct to conclude that the Croatian population compared to the Muslim one was a small minority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it would be more exact to say that demographically, the Croat population had an inferior number than the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this statistical piece of information important?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on the use that you want to -- not you personally, policymakers, wanted to have. This can be, you know, just knowledge, in this sense. I would like to stress -- let me say -- this is very important question. Sometimes the rights of the groups, of ethnic groups, are related to have more rights or less right to the number of a group. But I think this is not correct. Right is right. You can be ten, you can be 10 million. A right is a right. If a group has a right to be protected, this right does not depend on the number of persons in a group. Unfortunately this is used now even in the Kosovo question. So the Albanians are claiming -- or Macedonia, they are 20 percent, 30 percent, 40 percent, but if there is right of the Albanians to be protected as a collective, it doesn't matter whether they are 20 percent or 40 percent. So significant or not, it depends on the use that policymakers make in this sense, you know, because otherwise this is -- can be just to know the structure of the population as well as, you know, for instance, when you receive the figures of the birth rates, of the death rates, they are figures. It depends on the use you make.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree with you, Professor. I would kindly ask the usher to present the exhibit number 39. Professor Bianchini, could you just explain the source of this map for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map that I suggested to be prepared by the officers here, the Tribunal, under my control, taking into consideration generally the census results, and other maps that I collected from different books and sources, they were published, and there are different ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the map is based on data collected from the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the census of 1991, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, the area covered also in the indictment covers the area of municipality of Vitez and Busovaca, it's somewhere in the centre of the map, you can look at them there. Could you comment, Sir, in view of the logic of this map, what is the composition of the population here, particularly in view of the surrounding areas, namely, the municipalities which surround municipality Vitez and Busovaca, particularly Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Another atlas I have, because I can give better ... This is a very good atlas published in Croatia, and this is one of my sources. And here in the atlas there are the lists of the municipalities of Bosnia and Croatia with the results of the census in this area. So you ask me about Vitez and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, let us focus on this map which has been presented as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you have a context, you see the colour is showing that the percentage of a certain number of ethnic groups is more or less than the 50 percent of each area, and in this sense, you see, as, for instance, for Vitez, that population was below Croatian population, below the 50 percent, this means that the other parts were shared by Muslims and Serbs. I would like to stress anyway that all these maps, all these maps -- I had the opportunity to see a lot of these maps -- can give you or to all of you just a general picture, very general picture, and I will explain why. Because if you consider the most red part, Livno, Duvno here, Tomislavgrad, Prozor, this area, you can have the idea that the Croatian population was overwhelmingly concentrated in this area, which is only to a certain extent true because in the balance of the ethnic -- of the demographic proportion, there were much more Croats in other areas, for instance in Sarajevo, in Central Bosnia, than here. But here there were less population so you have the 90 percent of Croats but the impact of this 90 percent is less important than the impact in the other parts because the population was much more higher in terms of hundreds of thousands of people living in one area than in the other. So in this case, I used this map just to give a general picture, but this general picture can offer to persons the exact context. So that's why, in the end, when you see the map, the map then, you have to refer to the tables or the census if you want to have the real structure of one district, for instance. Otherwise, you can't have from the maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand what you are trying to say, Professor, but let us go back to this exhibit which has been tendered as evidence. This map which you say was made on the basis of your instructions, according to the 1991 census. May we conclude, looking at this map, that the municipality of Busovaca is predominantly surrounded by a Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only to certain extent because you see that Kiseljak and other areas have predominant Croatian population, so -- and Fojnica has not so predominant population, they were in position in Fojnica, they were above 50 percent, but this is giving only the colour of the ethnic group who had the relative majority in this part, this means that the difference can be from the first to the second on the only 100 persons, you know, sometimes. So in this sense -- that's why, I repeat, the map can offer just a general picture but can't be considered in this sense -- only to certain extent you can conclude in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. I should like to ask the usher for exhibit number 42. This is yet another statistical table which depicts the composition of the Bosnia-Herzegovinan parliament in 1990 after the democratic elections. Can you tell us, Professor, whether this composition, and I'm referring particularly to the three dominant groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbs, the Muslims, and the Croats, whether this composition of representation in parliament actually reflects the picture of the representation of these national entities in the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because SDR, SDS, and HDZ were voted predominantly by their own relevant ethnic group, that is Muslims, Serbs and Croats. That is one of the reasons why concerns immediately increased in Bosnia because this was considered by many of the scholars as a vote based not predominantly on difference of ideas but only on ethnic reasons. And, you know, this vote radically overthrown the polls who were published by the newspapers before the elections were taken, they were opinion polls generally and they asked, and all the opinion polls generally predicted the victory of the Ante Markovic party which had, in fact, a great defeat in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So in a sense the result -- the outcome of the election were surprisingly enough for the population and for the public opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this percentage of members of parliament reflect the political clout that they had in parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly you mean with this sentence in the sense that you have -- you can see -- if you refer to the percent of seats or you refer to the exact ability to influence the government and the decision-making in the presidency and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the seats in parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have a percentage -- if you can make a comparison, the percentage of SDR is 37.8 percent, the Muslims generally were around 43 percent, so a little bit less, but the great majority is there. The SDS received the 26.5 percent, and the Serbs were 34 percent, and the Croats 14.7 percent, they were a little bit less than 18. And so in this sense more or less they reflected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps just to clarify one point. In what way were decisions taken in the Bosnian and Herzegovinian parliament at the time, what was the system of decision making, was it out voting by the majority or by a consensus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was one of the quarrels all the time, that's why the government and the parliament were not effective in their decisions, because on the one side, particularly from the Serb point of view, there were claimed consensus. Very interesting question because the Serbs were against the consensus in the Yugoslav federation but they claimed consensus in the Bosnian context. So the approach of the ethnic policy was that very pragmatically they used the tools, the instruments in order to protect themselves so the Serbs were for the proportion of voting in Yugoslavia on the basis of the fact that they were the 36 percent of the population. While in Bosnia, when they understood that SDR and HDZ had the possibility to vote together, in main opportunity it happened and they had the majority, the SDS didn't participate in the vote in the assembly, they didn't boycott the vote and then declare the vote was not correct and fair, and claimed the consensus. So in this sense, we can see that the parliament and the government were unable to do effective policies in the period between 1990 and 1992, and even the passing of the law was extremely difficult when it happened for this reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Professor, for how long did the Bosnian parliament actually and substantially function, this particular one that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say that generally, if we speak about the majority, we can -- the majority of the members taking part today -- to the parliament, it -- this parliament had the opportunity to work until the beginning of the war, that is the period until April 1992, and then it was of course impossible because the clashes in Sarajevo start immediately and the city was surrounded and besieged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what we are talking about right now, the functioning of the parliament, was discontinued, we can take it, with the besieging of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the fact, however, is it has to be considered that this was the legal parliament.
