It was the condition, the external condition, hindered to work, but this was at least recognised as a legal parliament, so only new elections can change this one, and this follow the reason why the international community claimed immediately after the Dayton agreement, new elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. I should like to ask the usher for exhibit number 108. These are the results of the referendum in Bosnia. Would you just briefly, Professor, remind us of what kind of referendum that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already spoke in the previous session about the referendum, and I explained that the referendum was on a -- based on a question approved by the parliament of Bosnia in January 1992 where the Serb, SDS, didn't take part, and the question was -- we can reread, but you have evidence in this sense, that people was asked if they wanted to stay in a sovereign independent state of citizens and peoples while, I repeat, the HDZ submitted from Livno another proposal which created concern and tensions in relations with SDA in which the terms citizens were completely erased and remained as a sovereign state of the three titular nations in their own cantons. This was the -- so even the question remained that voted by the parliament, as far as I know, I don't know if some other question was more or less really written in other areas proposed, but this remained. It's clear that from the mentality -- if you take into consideration the mentality of the policymakers who suggested to vote for independence, moved from two different point of view at least to a large extent, particularly because in HDZ, Kljujic was overthrown in February 1992, that is in the same month when the Livno question was submitted by HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Generally speaking, was this a referendum for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not -- we can't restrict this question only on these terms. This was a referendum on the independence -- on a sovereign independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina of citizens and peoples, and I would like to emphasise particularly this question, the citizenship, because this is a very important element. In order to balance the influence of the collective rights which have not to be denied. But in order to not to have a only predominant role of the collective rights over the individual rights, so in this sense I think that we can restrict the question as you ask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was there -- were there consequences of this referendum also in the state and legal field the proclamation of sovereign state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now if we look at the percentage of voters in the referendum in your statement, you say that the Serb population did not turn out, the majority of the Serb population did not turn out at the referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Journalists, scientists, scholars, and policymakers, this is the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we take into consideration the fact that apart from the Serb population, apart from some minor groups, there also lived the Muslim and Croatian populations in Bosnia, the result of the voting from the existing electorate are 63.5 percent, what does that percentage cover in your interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This 63.95 percent of, yes, of eligible voters, means that was a large part of population -- the overwhelming population belonging to the Croatian and Muslim community plus -- plus other persons, maybe -- probably Yugoslavs, other minorities, Jews, and other minorities who had a peculiar role in the Bosnian context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If now we go back to the statistical result of the ethnic representation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and see that in 1991 -- that is exhibit number 38.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to follow you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if we look at the percentage of the Muslim population, which is 43.7, and 17.3 being the percentage of the Croatian population which, taken together, is 61 percent? Can we derive from that the conclusion that actually the 63.95 percent of the total electorate of Bosnia-Herzegovina in it, it was mostly or perhaps exclusively the Muslims and the Croatians that voted in favour of a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims and Croatian population take part in this, but it's impossible to conclude exactly in this sense because the ballot was secret and because we don't know how voted the Yugoslavs as well as you see the 5.5 percent, the others are the 1.1 percent. So they had also an influence in this vote, and I think that one part of them -- of this -- a large part of this ethnic groups are national declarations, as you can include, I don't know, the Yugoslavs participate in the vote. So generally yes, not exactly -- not making a direct amount of the -- just the Muslim and the Croats and just a group of the others because we can't -- we can't exclude that the other -- the other minorities also participate and the ballot was secret, so we can conclude that the overwhelming majority of Serbs voted against the overwhelming majority of the Muslims and the Croats opted for <?>.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask for exhibit number 109. Professor, Sir, in your exposition you also showed this table and you did say that as a reservation that there were no exact data and that you also quoted some of the sources because of that. Can you just, observing this table only very generally say what was the ratio between the forces, the numerical ratio between the forces of the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims in relation to these elections -- to these sources,<the interpreter corrects herself>?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see very clearly on the map when you see that, for instance, the Bosnian Muslims, according to different sources, were between 100,000 and two hundred, so more than 200,000, while Croatian army was reduced (?) by something between 30 and 65,000, so -- the number is different but the weapons that the army had was different --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are not data --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Missed answer).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we then conclude that these racial forces ranged between 1 to 2 to 1 to 3 1/2 to 4 in favour of the Muslims? Will the usher please bring exhibit number 114, 114. Professor, this is a map of the Yugoslav state from 1918. In giving evidence yesterday, you said that the geographical maps and borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina which is shown in the centre of the map since that time to the unfortunate events in the former Yugoslavia has not changed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the borders that you can see here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The republican border of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina was not a republic, it was just an area in 1918, so they are today more or less international borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, more or less these are more or less the same, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here in this map we can see that Bosnia-Herzegovina has access to the sea, the Boca Korduska bay to the south of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never. You can see this is -- this is not a Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes, yes. This was the only -- only -- only connection with the seaside was here with Nieljna, the other is just ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell us then what is this outlet, this access to the sea drawn in the Boca Korduska bay, is that a mistake or should one interpret it differently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this is mistake. I don't have evidence about a Bosnia-Herzegovina that had in that area a sea connection, the sea in that area. I don't have this kind of evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we then conclude that this is not a correct datum that has been drawn in this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you want, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask the usher for exhibit number 116. Exhibit 116 -- there are several, A to E, I believe. We shall now confine ourselves to 116 A, this first map, drawn on that paper. The title is the ethnic division of Bosnia agreed by the three national parties in the Villa Konak. Would you just briefly remind us what kind of a meeting that was and who took part in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a meeting that was organised immediately after the referendum in order to -- before the -- sorry, it was -- yes, yes, immediately after the referendum, and it was an attempt at finding a solution before erupting the war, so the representative of the three national parties, SDS, HDZ, and SDA took part in preparing this agreement which was an agreement that in the end didn't -- was -- didn't work. So it was one of the last attempts, generally speaking, I don't think that it was particularly important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, Sir, do you perhaps remember the participants in the meeting? Who was there? Who attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you perhaps remember, if I remind you that Mr. Mate Boban, Mr. Izetbegovic, and Mr. Radovan Karadzic were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can check if you want.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether any international organisation had any sort of a patronage over that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems to me that the European union was even urging, particularly in connection with the attempt of Cutilieo, it was connected to the Cutiliero proposal of cantonisation of Bosnia which was submitted in February 1992 to the authorities of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in respect of this map that we have before us, can you comment on that map in relation to the plans which were made subsequent to it with the objective of calming tensions in Bosnia and Herzegovina and its division into cantons, that of the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what can I add of what I already said in this sense. This was an ethnic division that was not the only claim of -- for the organisation of Bosnia. Then the other question was, what can be the organisation -- the political organisation of -- within these cantons and how can the cantons related to each other, so there were many other questions, it was not just a question of maps. The question of maps was important, but this was only one of the disputed issues between the parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made reference in the beginning to the fact that at this meeting under the patronage of the European community, Mr. Cutiliero in cooperation with the representatives of the three dominant nations in Bosnia, tried to resolve the situation on the basis of an ethnic division in Bosnia. That is what is written on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there are three national parties, yes, on the basis of the three national parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ethnic division.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, my personal opinion is, and this is one of the reasons why the international community shared responsibilities in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, is that the international community, particularly at that moment the European community, supported to a certain extent the idea of creating ethnic areas in Bosnia. This was one of the reasons why this created concern, because this is important to take into consideration. While Serb and Croat parties, SDS and HDZ, at that moment agreed in a sense to have ethnic cantons, this was not so clear for the Muslims and the others. There were fundamentalists and there were extremes as they are thinking about the possibility to accept these ideas, and this has remained for all the time in Bosnia, until today, while another stream of the SDA plus those that were not included in the let me say three ethno-national parties, belonging to other parties were against this partition, they opposed, and they opposed for this reason, because they didn't want to have cantons on the basis of ethnic regions. They could accept ideas and there were projects of areas, cantons, with an economic, cultural, common -- economic, cultural basis, but not ethnic basis, but not predominant ethnic basis. This explained why. Because of the war, for a long period, SDR, has received a positive stereotype, generally, of defending the integrity of Bosnia because he was supported by these democrats because of the wars or against the Serbs then during 1993-94 against HVO and the Croats but, but, this is now, after the war, more became clear that it was not so evident this alliance between the two because they was a part in the SDA which opposed and which was ready to accept the idea of the so-called Muslimania, that is a restricted state where the Muslim live together without Serbs and Croats and the problem again was the map, because this Muslimania will have an outlet toward the river, toward the Adriatic sea, toward both areas or not, this was an open question, and this was an extreme within the SDA. So you know that even recently many disputed issues were opened in Sarajevo and even Izetbegovic was charged because of what happened in Sarajevo in 1992-'93 because of the Saso case or I can mention here the rethinking of the war by Causevic, for instance, or the charge of the General<?> against Izetbegovic. What does it mean, all this? Now, after the war, it is becoming clear that even in the SDR, there was this extreme pressing for accepting this kind of partition where another part was against, and for this reason it was possible a cooperation with the democrats. Otherwise, this was -- now it is appearing clear that this relation was a disputed relation in many respects. So this is -- the question, the future of Bosnia has to be considering this -- in this complex context where the SDA had often a very unbalanced position and changed often its opinion because of the relations of the extremes within the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I'm sorry to be interrupting you now, but I propose a break. I also apologise to Professor Bianchini, but we will have a recess of 15 minutes. Thank you. ---Recess taken at 11..57 a.m. --- Resumed at 12.17 p.m. (The accused entered court) (Proceedings begin - no translation) THE DETAINEE: Yes, sir, everything's all right. I just didn't feel well for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I have noticed that you don't seem to feel very well, but I believe we may resume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, shall we now return to the map we have on the ELMO. May we conclude that this map is a consequence of the negotiations held in Vijakonic between Mr. Boban, Mr. Izetbegovic, and Mr. Karadzic under the patronage of the European Union and that resulted in this solution based on the ethnic division of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To a certain extent, yes. To certain extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the usher to submit -- to tender as evidence exhibit 119. Please leave the exhibit 116, leave it so that we can draw a comparison. I would kindly ask the usher to return exhibit number 116 in order to be able to draw a comparison. But we will also go through the other exhibits 116. Professor, we have the exhibit 119. Could you give us an explanation, what is it about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... Partition of -- proposal of distribution of the cantons in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan, as a result of the plan, we have this map. And it goes between January and -- yes, it was submitted January -- 2nd of January 1993. The Vance-Owen Plan represents an attempt of the international community to resolve the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina; true? If we compare the two maps, can we conclude that also the Vance-Owen Plan gives an indication of a solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina on the basis of an ethnic division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To a large extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we say, at least as far as these documents are concerned that have been tendered as evidence, that there is an observable trend in the international community to resolve -- to wish to address the question in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the ethnic principle at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a sense, yes. In a sense, yes. In a sense, yes. This is why I think that the international community shared responsibilities for the war in this area for a certain period, yes. It's true that -- it's true that in any case this must be added, that when the international community try -- because the position of the international community was ambiguous enough, as often the policymakers are, ambiguous enough in order to support, on one side, a redistribution of the cantons in the area given a particular importance to the ethnic majority group in this area and the protection -- because this was all the times confirmed that Bosnia was a sovereign state within its own -- its internationally recognised border and had to remain in a sense a state within these international recognised border. So this is important, also to stress, in order to understand the ambiguity of the position of the international community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this ethnic principle is always there. It is just a question of the technique of the division of the cantons between the three dominant populations in Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To a large extent exact while this was -- I would like to insist on this aspect. I'm sorry. You see, I have the impression that if we insist only on the aspect of the-- as the international community did to resettle Bosnia on the basis of ethnic principles and to establish the map as a map of -- based on these principles, we have the clear impression that the war in Bosnia anyway was a war amongst three ethnic groups with their own army, with their own flags, symbols, the Croat Muslim and the Serbs. I would like to stress that this is true but only partially true. Only partially true. This approach, which was, to a large extent, supported by international community, and this is why, I repeat, they share responsibility, it's only partially true because there happened a second war simultaneously during that period, and this was the war against civilian populations, no nationalists, anti-nationalists, living in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those who didn't want to accept the ethnic predominant role in the organisation of the state. This is not a case that the war started symbolically with the Serb snipers shooting against pacifist people demonstrating in Sarajevo for a united Bosnia. And if you think all the evolution of the war, ethnic cleansing, the cases of rapes, offensive against civilian populations was very clear the sign. I mentioned today even the attempt at creating homogenised group in order to establish a prerequisite for war. Because this was a prerequisite, it had to be implemented during the war, and the war was an instrument, a tool for joining this result. So the war between the three ethnic groups was a war for -- between -- or amongst three nationalist conceptions that they shared the same mentality, the same mechanism of evaluating the maps in Bosnia, you know. And they couldn't agree on the borders. While all of them had their own internal war against a part of the population of their own group in order to impose this ethnic organisation. So I think this can also be stressed in order to understand the tragic situation of Bosnia and the reason why a lot of people fled the country and this was not only displaced poor people but particularly who fled the country in Bosnia; as well as in Croatia and in Serbia, there were people with a medium or high knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, Sir, just for the sake of clarification, would you please be so kind as to take another look at exhibit 116, the maps under letters B to E. Can you explain to us what the maps are these and what is the source of the data?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a comparative study made by --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The sources --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- in a book published in Spain. And they prepared these maps and they published the study in Valencia in 1992 or 1993-- 1993 1993 after a conference that was held there, so immediately after the erupting of the war in Bosnia. So this is the result of a group of scholars coming from different countries, United States, Spain, Serbia, and other countries. And they made this -- they published these maps in order to make clear which was the position of the three -- of the three groups when -- what about the areas that they were interested in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Yes, we can put away exhibit number 116. Will the usher please present exhibit number 117 to Professor Bianchini? This chart shown on document number 117, you said was published in the magazine Dani. Can you say to us where is this magazine published, who is it published by, and what is the credibility of this magazine generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... Dani September 1997, so you can easily find the document. The magazine is published in Sarajevo, it's a magazine which has generally attracting attention of people. About this document, I had the opportunity to read the documentation and the original and I can say that what was published by Dani was the document effectively. So, you know, sometimes I'm not so -- particularly me, when I'm finding the sources, I am interested to know if the sources are correct -- yes, available, but I don't see if the magazine is popular -- sometimes I found excellent things also reading books that can be, for instance, with a cultural, ideological ideas far from mine. Generally I don't look at these, but I try to see if the document is a document that is reported accurately or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know where the Dani magazine got this chart from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This -- I don't know why and how they received it. I know that the document they published and there were polemics in dispute-- disputation in Bosnia when they published this document, and I think that it's better maybe to ask directly to the journalists. This I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I can gather, so we are talking about a document which was just carried by the magazine Dani and we do not know the sources of the magazine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... The document was published that the source is OSCE. I can't -- I can't say who the persons or who gave personally, but as stated in Dani and as is written, if you look at the document published -- they published and translated only certain parts, not completely the document, but they made a kind of opening page where it is written that the source is OSCE, as reported here, Mission for Bosnia. This is original in central Mostar, so this was prepared evidently in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you, as you've said, this document was prepared by the OEC. Was it also published in the official documents of the OEC in their report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ( No audible answer).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the usher to bring to the professor exhibit number 118.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: I don't think the last question of counsel's was answered. The question was: Have you, as you've said, this document was prepared by the OEC, was it also published in the official documents of the OEC in their report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour, for intervening on this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now we have in front of us document 118 representing the conclusions adopted in Grude on the 12th of November, 1992. The conclusions of a meeting. How would you describe that meeting? What kind of a meeting was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a meeting as reported in the document between representative of the regional community of Herzegovina and the Regional Community of Travnik. The persons who participate in the meeting are listed in the last page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's not disputed. I would like to focus on the original and the heading and also the translation, the upper part, left-hand corner. And this heading represents the heading of a political party, the Croatian Democratic Union?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is written here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we say therefore that this document resulted from a party meeting of the Croatian Democratic Union?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, you've already commented, this document I would like to ask you to comment on something else. Please go to page 2, item 3. Point 3, sub point (a). Could you comment on this part of the text, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the sentence where it is written clearly defined to the party policy of HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina strengthen the party with new staff and select those people who will be able to carry out these tasks completely. In my opinion, this has to be taken into account that as a strong criticism at the time president of HDZ, Stjepan Kljujic. This was -- so on the basis of the conclusion, they, evidently, thought that Kljujic was not able to carry out these tasks completely, at least completely. So this is my conclusion considering what happened later, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. But I'm really interested in the fact whether such a conclusion, does it lead us to the conclusion concerning the organisation of -- the internal organisation of a political party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The political party already existed, so this was an evident claim to reorient in a sense or better implement party policy in order to achieve the goals described before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So political goals through a political party. Item (b), point (b), would you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initiate political and legal actions in the country and abroad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that lead us in the same direction of political proclamation of the political goals of HDZ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It can be in a sense because both parties, particularly because you have to take into account the culture of the -- if I well understand your question, the culture of the time was conditioned and influenced by a specific culture, which was the culture of the Communist time when the difference between institutions and party were not so clear and evident as it was or is in Western Europe, for instance. So I can imagine that people thinking on a party and a party -- because HDZ as well as SDS, as well as in a sense SDA, were the peculiar party. They were not only organisations of ideas, they were organisation for protecting an ethnic group, they were an organisation trying to protect this group through political and military tools. So the bonds between these aspects were not so evident and clear as we can imagine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will remind you of the period when this meeting was held and that was November 1991. It was the period when the Biaac parliament was operating; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I add that this day is the day when the first Croatian community of Posavina was proclaimed, November 12th, interesting enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, Sir, I believe you have exhibit number 119 or, if not, you will be receiving it shortly. So this refers to the Vance-Owen Plan. Could you briefly give us a chronology how this plan was being drawn up, how did it end, by whom it was signed, and how did the situation evolve? Give a picture to the trial chamber of the situation on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... Prepared, submitted by the two international mediators Owen and Vance, and it was generally supported immediately by the Croatian side. The Muslim side and the SDR, it was uncertain but in the end accepted and what is interesting is it was accepted by the Serb side, by Karadzic and Milosevic while -- and this is very interesting -- in the end when Karadzic went to the parliament of the SDS in the area under the control of the Serb side, the majority was against. In order to help and to define the positive reactions, Milosevic, with Prime Minister Mitsotakis from Greece, went to Bosnia in order to ask the representative of SDS to approve the parliament, while the patriarch of Serbia, Pavle, supported the rejection of the plan and the plan was rejected. Then they organised a referendum, if I well remember, in the Serb part of -- controlled part of Bosnia. And the referendum of course rejected the plan. So in this case, the Serb -- this happened in May, however. If I well remember, the meeting with Mitsotakis was at the beginning of May 1993, just to give you -- so the discussion was -- and then rejected and then they started again to rediscuss the problem. And in July Owen and Stoltenberg submitted another proposal while Vance resigned. This was the story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, Sir, do you remember who were the negotiators in Geneva when discussing, under the auspices of Mr. Owen and Vance, who were the negotiators of the national entities of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's interesting that if I well remember, there was not only a discussion among the representatives of SDS, HDZ, SDA, Radic, Izetbegovic, and if I well remember, Mate Bobin but also there were the representatives of Croatia and Serbia, Tudjman and Milosevic who took part in these discussions for the Vance Owen as well for the Owen Stoltenberg plan, so they were invited and participated in discussions, both of the presidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the majority populations from Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were Boban, Izetbegovic, and Karadzic, those that participated in the drafting of the Cutiliero plan in Villa Konic true? What conclusion can we draw in this continuity? What kind of continuity of the negotiators from Bosnia and the idea from abroad, the first plan, the Konic plan, and Mr. Cutiliero, and the second plan, the Vance-Owen plan, where the international community tried to resolve the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two different points of view. Two different point of view. The internal point of view was that HDZ, SDR, and SDS claimed to be the only representatives of each group, and they participated to these maps and to this discussion as the representatives of these three parts in conflict. While from the international community point of view, the approach was much more -- was different and again ambiguous. They don't -- they supported the integrity of Bosnia, and this is clear. All the time they repeated this. At the same time, they were a stream, I may say at the time a main stream in the international community that was of the opinion that in a way we have to find a compromise amongst the three parts, so Karadzic, the SDS, HDZ, in order to stop the war. And for this reason, they tried to think of a compromise. This was, in my opinion, a great political mistake, but thinking that it was possible to find a mediation and a solution on the basis of the territorial, political, historical, cultural, economical claim of these three parties, but saving at the same time the integrity, the independence and the integrity of Bosnia. This was the different approach. I want to stress this because albeit I insisted on the responsibility of the international community in their internal -- in the war in the former Yugoslavia and, in this case, in Bosnia, I'm insisting that even Vance Owen share this responsibility. However, the last choice, the last decisions were -- became from inside, and it was the inner situation of these three political parties that created the condition, and they use manipulating interpreting only the part that was interesting for them in this kind of mediation, forgetting completely the aspect connected to the sovereignty, independent state within the international recognised border. This was a question not not in evidence. Sometimes they reported the sentence because it was obliged from the international context, but the interest was particularly to turn attention to this, to implement this aspect, so they used this part of the international relation approach for their own war goals while the international community thought, in my opinion making mistake, but this is my opinion, of course -- thought that it was possible to combine a mediation amongst the three parties by saving the integrity of whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina, integrity and the integrity for reasons, international reasons that they had, the integrity and independence of Bosnia in its internationally recognised borders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, Sir, let us remind of the chronology of the Vance-Owen plan. First it was signed by the party headed by Mate Boban on the 4th of January, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The support was in immediate --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that the Muslim representatives signed on the 21st of March and that Karadzic signed it later on, but he had a reservation that it had to be approved by the parliament and then the referendum was held which turned down and rejected the Vance-Owen Plan; true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even the parliament, the Serb parliament rejected, not only the referendum. The referendum was made after, anyway, but even the -- the assembly, Serb assembly, rejected it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, considering this map in front of you, exhibit 119, could you tell us, Sir, in accordance and in line with the Vance-Owen Plan which is a continuation of the Villa Konic plan, under whose authority are Vitez and Busovaca in this cantonal division?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I'm looking well, they are in the canton number 10?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Canton number 10? And canton number 10 ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was one of the three cantons it considered connected to the Croatian majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask the usher to present exhibit number 121. Generally speaking, Professor, for familiarisation purposes, do you know when the HVO was founded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, formally 8 April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when the army of BiH was formally established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Halilovic became the head of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the end of May, May 25th, 1992, so later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So approximately a month and a half later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Army of Bosnia was created through different groups that were connected so this was a process that was -- that takes more or less around one month and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at any rate, we are speaking about the period from -- somewhere around the half of 1992 when that period of time is transferred from Bosnia to Croatia. What do we have in Croatia in that particular period? What is the state of affairs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have tensions and a situation of tensions, but not a situation of open war. We are in 1992, we have already the peacekeepers, UN peacekeepers in Krajina, and we have the cease-fire, and particularly a concern of the Croatian authorities about the future and the protections of southern Dalmatia, that means particularly Dubrovnik and the area of Dalmatia, in this sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time -- I withdraw the question. I shall rephrase my question. When did the war in Croatia begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war started -- it's important to -- sorry. The war started on June 27th in Slovenia, and then it was -- this is the same war --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it's the same war. From Slovenia, this war involved Croatia, so I think it is more correct to say it involved parts of Croatia in the war, this happened between -- in August-September 1991, and this war -- this part of the war, the conflict lasted until the cease-fire was complied with and the peacekeepers of the UN took their -- were deployed in Krajina. But this is one phase because, as you know, there were other actions in order -- organised by the army of Croatia in order to free areas considered part of Croatia. This was -- the first was the question of the -- of Peruca, then Maslenica, then Slavonia, then Krajina. This was western Slavonia and Krajina, yes. This was just a part, we can say a more tragic and more dramatic part. The worst period for Croatia was particularly between August and January-February, August of 1991, January-February of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, we are aware of the fact that in the very least, one needs two parties to have a war. Can you tell us what parties were involved in the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: JNA, still at that time called the JNA, i.e. the army, the Yugoslav army, which was under a process of transformation. But the process of transformation didn't end at the time, and the organised members of the Croatian army, Territorial Defence, several groups that were connected with the so-called Zbor Narodne Garde and then became the Croatian army. So they were even in Croatia preparing themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we have on the one hand the war in Croatia with the JNA attacking and then we have attempts at creating, establishing the Croatian army through this Zbor Narodne Garde National Garde Corps; can you tell us at that period in Bosnia Herzegovina the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, whether there were any indications, any hints in Bosnia-Herzegovina of future war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... I have spoken about that when I was here. A series of tensions, of events that created concerns and difficulties. I remember the mobilisation of JNA in Bosnian Krajina in September. In October there was the attack on Ravno by JNA --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm speaking the fall of 1991, fall of 1991. In November the bridges on the Sava river were mined and other clashes took place between February-March 1992. So until September 1991, the situation was, in a sense, managed, and then there started a series of tensions that were to increase in the months to come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, Sir, so at the time of these events, do you, as a historian and an expert on the area, recall the statement of Mr. Izetbegovic who was commenting on the war in Croatia said, "That is not our war."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A lot of statements were made in this sense by different policymakers. I remember very well --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The sentence was clear because at that moment Izetbegovic was -- I repeat, in a very uncertain position. I mention even his intention to consider the possibility of Bosnia remaining in the Yugoslav federation and whether Serbia and Croatia together would join this federation. But this was a statement very clear disputed on other occasions. I remember very clearly when the war started in Slovenia, the Slovene policymakers were deeply offended by the attitude of the Bosnia-Herzegovinan policymakers because they more or less still used this term. It's quite understandable. I think that they know very well that the dismemberment of Yugoslavia meant the dismemberment of Bosnia and the war in Bosnia. . So they try with this statement to outline a different context and different fate for Bosnia when Bosnia was, in fact, the focus of the war and it was evidently clear in 1990, 1989-1990, that if Yugoslavia were dismember the war would be particularly hard and bloody in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That was the generally held opinion but it was not correct, unfortunately. As for the representatives of the dominant Muslim population in Bosnia and Herzegovina in relation to the coming war, you said yesterday that the JNA, in pulling out, had given orders, even before, that the weapons were to be taken out of the depots of the arms and armaments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- was signed by Borisav Jovic as president of the presidency of Yugoslavia on May the 23rd, 1990, at the request of Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This order to take out of the Territorial Defence depots was implemented in Bosnia-Herzegovina ... That JNA managed to take other weapons from the Territorial Defence storehouses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Answered interrupted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, apart from the ordinance, the weapons of the JNA, there were no other weapons in Bosnia-Herzegovina (TALKING SIMULTANEOUSLY) apart from personal weaponry, of course. I'm talking about organised weaponry, legal arms --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1990 or 1991, in between these two years, no. Organisation and army organisation didn't exist in this period, in between 1990 and 1991, no. This was -- I remember that -- I stressed, emphasised that this was even a charge against Milosevic -- against Izetbegovic, sorry, later when the war ended on the basis of the fact that accepting this decision of the presidency, he dismantled the possibility of Bosnia to defend itself. But, you know, ex-post you can make a lot of considerations. It is interesting to say the consideration that arose in Bosnia after the war in 1995,'96,'7 when they started to ask, maybe it was a mistake to ask the -- to become sovereign independent state and it was better to establish a particular relation with the Serb side, as it was originally suggested. For instance, by a Muslim policy maker, Adil Zulfikarpasic, as you remember, and the answer was that instead of having immediately the war with the Serb side, as it happened in Bosnia in April 1992, we had the war with the Croat side which would never have accepted staying in a federation with Serbia. So you can have a lot of speculation ex post on this situation. It was, in fact, very difficult because of the context, of the Yugoslav context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier you said that in March 1992, there was held a referendum which was preceded by the proclamation, promulgation of the constitution of the Serb republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you want, I can obtain an exact date because I have the constitutions. You asked me the Serb constitution in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- here it's written in 1992. It was amended in September 1992, the constitution, so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know when the Serb deputies in Sarajevo promulgated the constitution of the Serb republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately it's written that the constitution of the republic was approved in 1992 but not the month, so I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Will you tell us, Professor, to sum up. So at that time the JNA emptied the warehouses of the Territorial Defence, and on the 8th of April, 1992, the HVO was established a bit later, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established. Why were these armies founded? We assume, although that has not been said, that the third party, the Serbs, were also undertaking certain steps. Can you describe in brief that so that we can have an impression of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The recognition on April 6th, 1992, the JNA started operation activities, so this was an evident responsibility that started from this side. And in this sense, they were operating, in a sense, that they wanted to move from the eastern and western side in order to isolate the line from Mostar to Sarajevo (TALKING SIMULTANEOUSLY).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the strategic objective. Who opposed that strategic objective in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You had on the one side different position in this situation of confusion. Most unprepared were the Muslims and the anti-nationalists, the pacifists. They wanted and they organised the demonstrations in Sarajevo in order to save the integrity of Bosnia, so this was their strategy of Bosnia. While, if your question is connected particularly on the area of Herceg-Bosna, when HVO was created. The HVO was created first to protect the Croat people in the area, where Croats were living.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (No answer).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A while ago, you said that they were prepared for the imminent war of which fact many were not aware at the time were the Muslims and the anti-nationalists. Were any measures, any military actions, being taken at that time vis-à-vis the attacks which were coming from the JNA and the Serb paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... They reacted on the basis of what they had. For instance, it existed already some group, even group connected to the Territorial Defence with some weapons or groups connected with the so-called Zelene Beretke, the Green Berets. It's a group --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And other organisations that in the end were organised in the so-called army of Bosnia. And the same HVO started in Italy when it was created to resist the action. But there is no doubt that the fact that the JNA backed irregular Serbs in that period made possible for the Serbs to control the 70 percent of the territory of Bosnia by the end of the year, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, will you please tell us what were the legal possibilities for purchasing and procuring arms for that particular area in that particular period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just remind you, in September 1991, the United Nations imposed an arms embargo for the area of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I already explained, the only possibility to obtain the weapons was for the Serb declaration side to receive the weapons from Serbia and Croatia respectively; while for the others they were in a situation -- in a kind of pocket, and so they had less opportunities -- evidently less opportunity in order to have this --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under such circumstances, who was actually -- who actually had available, could use the weapons which were available in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To a large extent all the republics, “republics" means in this case Serbia, these areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when Mr. Izetbegovic proclaimed a state of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was that on the 22nd of June in 1992, do you remember that date? Is it right that it was proclaimed, the state of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know when, but the situation --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was proclaimed. Can you comment on that. Why did Mr. Izetbegovic proclaim a state of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... This is evident because a war was dismembering the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: War. Who were the warring parties? Keep reverting to that but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... There were different situations. There were not only, only the Serbs against the Croats -- the Muslims and the Croats were in a, we can say, uneasy alliance but they were in alliance against the Serbs, but there was also a war against civilian populations. And this is very important because generally when we are thinking about the army, we think that the army was moving with -- as a normal war as, for instance, the Second World War or, you know, you have the -- an army against the other army and they are facing each other. This was not the case of Bosnia and of Yugoslavia generally, it was not only a war between two opposite forces. And it's not the case that the number of injured and victims is much more higher in -- with the civilians instead of the members of the army, the soldiers. So I think that it's important to understand that the war was a simultaneous war, which included the civilian population as a victim, but a victim which was in the political goals of the war situation, because the civilian population had to take part and to establish its own relation with one side, one ethnic side. Otherwise, they were displaced or refugees abroad, particularly abroad. Many people fled the country for this reason, and this is why -- is one of the reasons why refugees from outside former Yugoslavia have such difficulties to think of coming back again to their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you comment on or perhaps give your conclusion or your interpretation of this: Who was it really in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the area of the former Yugoslavia that was the most affected by UN arms embargo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to international opinions shared by the government of the United States, the Muslims were the more -- those who paid, who were more in difficulties for this, for this embargo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, Sir, you have before you document 121A. That is the order appointing General Janko Bobetko commander of the southern front. Can you, for the benefit of the Chamber, so that they could know what person we're talking about, give us a few facts about his previous life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can repeat what I already said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His political views, his orientation, his participation in previous historic events in the previous Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already explained and stated about Bobetko during the exhibit of the documents, so I explained that Bobetko was Tito's general. He was charged in Belgrade. He came back to Zagreb in the second half of the sixties. He participated in the nationalist movement in Croatia in 1970- '71. For this reason, he was, as all the leaders, policymakers of the Croat -- Croat League of Communists, he was expelled from political life, and he became in 1991 military advisor of the Croatian government when communism collapsed. And first he published some opinions on what was in Croatia in 1970-71. Then he was military advisor and then he was appointed by Tudjman as -- he was close to Tudjman. They knew each other very well -- very well since the '60s or '70s because of their common Communist past and because they shared the same political opinion during the Croatian crisis of 1970- '71.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now let's go back to the history back, Mr. Tudjman and General Bobetko took part in the Second World War fighting in the partisan ranks against the fascist occupying forces and anti-fascist orientation. That's what I'm speaking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (No answer heard by reporter).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, Sir, you have analysed all these documents which were as exhibit 121 of these documents, refer to the period from April to the second half 1992, approximately. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Between April --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between April and the first half of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Generally, yes. First half, yes, until July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us at the time, Sir, what war operations, military operations, were being carried out in Bosnia and Herzegovina or a colloquial question: Who was fighting against whom at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that period, you had the Croatian and Muslim alliance against the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, document 121F please, could you look at it? Here, at the beginning of the text of this document, under item number 1, we see the word "enemy." Who is the enemy here? To whom does this word apply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the Serb side, JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the same -- can the same be said also for the document 121M?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the area of Blaga Nevesinoe was subsequently on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now document 121N, does that also apply to the Serb side? Professor, Sir, in all these documents presented under exhibit number 121, have you found in your research work a document containing a command and order to act against the Muslims, the Muslim army, at that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (No answer heard by reporter).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we say that at the time, that period, when these documents were produced amongst Croats and Muslims, there were no tensions and no military conflicts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: The answer given by the professor to the question put to you has not been heard or reported. The question is: Have you found in your research work a document containing an order to act against the Muslims, the Muslim army, at that period? There is no answer recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The answer was "No."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question. As we were focusing on that period, when speaking of these orders and the exhibit number 121, what were the relations between Croatian and Muslim population? Were there any hostile military operations between the two entities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the military point of view, there were not tensions in this sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm thinking only of the military aspect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Sorry let me say, however, some tensions were growing in the Bosnian government, so if you speak about military, it's okay, but we have to take into account that there were concerns later and there were polemics between the Croatian and the Muslim side, particularly about the operation when Mostar was freed because Mostar was freed with contribution of the Croatian army and this has created concern in the government. So there were in this sense -- so this caused tensions under the skin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without military operations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's almost 1.30. I'd like to pass on to another series of questions, so the Defence would propose that we begin our hearing tomorrow with that series of questions, if you agree, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I believe that this is a good proposal of Mr. Mikulicic. We will adjourn for today and we will resume our deliberations tomorrow. We will see you tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
